results.title: GPU Rental Economics Face Pressure as Providers Seek New Revenue Models — Merkle.Press
highlights:
GPU rental prices are collapsing as supply outpaces demand, forcing infrastructure providers to explore hedging strategies and bundled services to maintain viable margins.

...

The infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence workloads has become increasingly commoditized, creating a structural tension between users seeking cheaper compute and providers holding expensive hardware. Companies building machine learning applications can access graphics processing units through rental marketplaces rather than purchasing equipment outright—a model that democratizes AI development but introduces margin compression for infrastructure operators. As spot prices for GPU capacity have declined significantly over the past eighteen months, providers face a profitability squeeze that mirrors similar dynamics seen in other utility-based computing markets. This economic pressure is forcing host operators to rethink their business models beyond simple per-unit-time pricing.

The fundamental issue stems from oversupply relative to actual demand. Multiple providers entered the GPU rental market simultaneously, including cryptocurrency-native platforms like Lambda Labs and traditional cloud operators expanding their service offerings. This competitive influx drove prices downward faster than utilization rates increased, creating an environment where providers struggle to achieve positive unit economics. A GPU server costing $30,000 to $50,000 requires sustained high utilization rates to justify its deployment, yet marketplace dynamics push rental rates lower just as adoption accelerates. This mirrors historical patterns in commoditized infrastructure markets, where price compression typically forces consolidation among providers with weaker cost structures.

Forward-looking operators are exploring hedging mechanisms and alternative revenue streams to stabilize cash flows. Some platforms are integrating tokenized derivatives that allow compute providers to lock in floor prices or maintain revenue certainty through financial instruments built on-chain. Others are bundling managed services, optimization software, or exclusive model access alongside raw compute, effectively shifting competition away from pure pricing toward value-added offerings. A few infrastructure-focused projects are experimenting with futures markets where GPU capacity itself becomes a tradeable asset with price discovery mechanisms. These approaches attempt to decouple provider revenue from spot market volatility while maintaining competitive pricing for end users.

results.title: GPU Rental Prices 2025-2026: How Fast They Move | Opengrid
highlights:
GPU rental prices used to be something you checked once a year. In 2025 and 2026 they moved by double digits in weeks. If you rent GPUs, the price you locked in last quarter may already be well above or below the market.

...

## The short version

| When | What happened | Move | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 Jun 2025 | AWS cuts its H100 on-demand price in a single announcement | −44% | AWS, via CloudZero and IntuitionLabs |
| Jun to Jul 2025 | Other providers follow with their own cuts, in single moves | −20% to −25% | CloudZero, IntuitionLabs |
| Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contract price climbs from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour | about +40% | SemiAnalysis |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | Silicon Data H100 rental index rises from $2.00 to $2.20 in four weeks | +10% | Silicon Data |
| 2026 | On-demand capacity sold out across all GPU types | n/a | SemiAnalysis |

In fifteen months the H100 went from a sharp price war to a shortage, with prices rising again.

...

It is nearly half the price, overnight, from the largest cloud provider in the world.

...

## Late 2025 into 2026: the reversal

Then the direction flipped.

- Contract prices rose about 40%. SemiAnalysis tracked one-year H100 contracts rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026.
- The rental index jumped 10% in four weeks. Silicon Data's H100 rental index went from $2.00 to $2.20 between December 2025 and January 2026.
- Capacity dried up. SemiAnalysis reported on-demand sold out across all GPU types in 2026, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027.

The teams that locked in contracts at the low point did well. The teams that waited paid 40% more for the same commitment a few months later.

...

It is tempting to think of "GPU prices" as one number. They are not. During the same stretch where the H100 rental index rose 10%, A100 and B200 prices stayed flat (Silicon Data).

Every GPU type has its own price band, and the bands are wide. Thunder Compute's September 2026 data:

| GPU | Price range, $ per hour |
| --- | --- |
| A100 | $1.09 to $5.07 |
| H100 | $2.89 to $11.06 |
| H200 | $3.44 to $10.60 |
| B200 | $3.50 to $27.04 |

Source: Thunder Compute, Sep 2026.

So "is now a good time to rent?" has no single answer. It depends on the chip, the provider and the pricing tier. For a provider-by-provider breakdown, see H100 price per hour in 2026.

## Price is not the only thing moving

Three other variables shift alongside the price:

- Capacity. A provider can be the cheapest on paper and have nothing available. With on-demand sold out across GPU types, finding capacity is often harder than finding a low price.
- Pricing tier. Spot runs 60% to 91% below on-demand, but the capacity can be pulled mid-job. Contracts are cheaper per hour but lock you in, and as above, contract prices can rise fast.
- The provider list itself. SemiAnalysis tracks 209 GPU clouds, up from 124. New supply keeps appearing, and it is spread across more places than anyone can check by hand.

...

Why are GPUs hard to rent in 2026?

SemiAnalysis reported on-demand capacity sold out across all GPU types in 2026, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027. Demand for AI training and inference is outpacing new supply.

results.title: GPU rental without hyperscalers: How good are neo clouds?
highlights:
At Lambda, an H100 GPU costs 3.55 euros an hour, against 10.95 euros at Azure, according to the price list of 4 October 2026. Neo clouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Lambda offer another option alongside hyperscalers. Several providers expand using secured loans. CoreWeave depends on a few large customers for much of its revenue.

...

For an hour on an Nvidia H100 GPU, the range on 4 October 2026 is wide. The rates are only comparable to a limited extent. Lambda charges the equivalent of 3.55 euros for the H100 SXM, calculated at the European Central Bank (ECB) reference rate of 2 October 2026. Nebius has been charging the equivalent of 4.01 euros since 1 October 2026, and CoreWeave charges the equivalent of 43.87 euros for a node with eight H100s, which works out at 5.48 euros per GPU. In the US East region, AWS charges the equivalent of 6.13 euros per GPU hour for the p5.48xlarge instance with eight H100s, according to the price tracker Vantage as of 3 October 2026. For the Azure VM ND96isr H100 v5, AzureSpeed lists the equivalent of 10.95 euros per GPU hour as of 26 September 2026 for Linux with usage-based billing in East US.

Scaleway has been charging 25.332 euros per hour for a node with eight H100 SXM since 1 June 2026, which works out at 3.17 euros per GPU. OVHcloud lists the H100 as a PCIe card at 2.80 euros net, while Lambda and Scaleway quote the SXM form factor.

...

On 1 October 2026, Lambda closed a loan equivalent to 898 million euros at 6.78 percent interest, secured by the financed GPU servers and the contractual cash flows from three deployments to two creditworthy buyers. Nscale, based in London, signed a GPU-backed credit facility equivalent to 1.25 billion euros on 12 February 2026. At the same time, Meta is planning a cloud business to sell surplus AI computing capacity, according to Reuters. cloudmagazin has classified this as a risk to CoreWeave and Nebius.

On 1 October 2026, Nebius raised the H100 hour from the equivalent of 3.43 to 4.01 euros, and the B200 from 6.37 to 7.57 euros. On 17 September 2026, CoreWeave reported short-duration contracts of three to six months at roughly 36 million euros in revenue per megawatt per year.

Neo clouds suit workloads with plenty of GPU time and little dependency on other cloud services: model training, fine-tuning and batch inference. results.title: Why a Three-Year-Old H100 Now Rents for More Than It Did on Day One
highlights:
In an AI chip market that refreshes constantly, last generation’s GPU has not fallen in price the way legacy hardware did. ‘The H100 batch we deployed in 2023 now rents for more than it did at launch,’ Stephen Balaban, co-founder and chief technology officer of cloud provider Lambda, said on The MAD Podcast.

...

The old hope was that GPU compute would standardise and cheapen like traditional cloud, with performance up and price down. AI compute has not followed that path. What one GPU delivers now depends on the system around it, how it coordinates with others, and whether the expensive hardware stays utilised. Chip performance still matters, but it rarely explains the compute a full stack delivers.

...

Frontier tasks rarely fit one GPU. Weights, compute and data split across many GPUs and servers, and a training or inference run lives or dies on how fast those GPUs exchange data. Same model, same count, same spec does not mean same compute, because network, memory, storage and software differ. That is why the supernode became a key AI-infra form: Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 wires 72 GPUs inside a rack over NVLink, and racks extend via InfiniBand or high-speed Ethernet. Lambda designs clusters to minimise network blocking.

The economics are heavy. Balaban estimates a gigawatt AI factory needs about US$ 2 billion to US$ 3 billion for power, US$ 10 billion to US$ 15 billion for the data-centre shell, and US$ 35 billion to US$ 45 billion for servers and compute, with the GPU the largest slice. In a GPU-hour’s cost, depreciation dominates. A roughly six-year accounting life is not the real economic life; an H100 that still takes jobs and finds renters can out-earn the market’s early guess.

...

There are at least three clocks on a GPU: product iteration (is it newest), accounting depreciation (how cost is spread), and economic life (how long it still earns). At 50 per cent utilisation, the depreciation loaded onto each working hour roughly doubles, because an idle GPU keeps depreciating. A 10,000-GPU cluster also needs CPU servers, storage and several networks, and scheduling software decides whether costly physical kit becomes on-demand compute at all.

results.title: Compute Futures Go Live: What the First GPU-Hour Price Curve Says About the AI Buildout — newscms
highlights:
On October 5, 2026, a commodity that has never been traded anywhere starts trading. The New York Mercantile Exchange, the clearing arm of CME Group, begins listing two futures contracts tied to the hourly rental price of a single AI accelerator: the Nvidia H100, the chip at the center of the current training and inference economy, and the Blackwell-generation B200 that is displacing it.

The contracts are financially settled, so no GPU changes hands. Each one covers 730 GPU-hours — one accelerator for roughly one average month — and settles against a daily index published by Silicon Data, a benchmarking firm backed by the trading firm DRW. They are the H100 and B200 rental index futures, announced in August by CME Group and Silicon Data together and listed on NYMEX pending CFTC review.

...

The B200 rental index, SDB200RT, entered September at $5.62 per GPU-hour, up 27.6% year to date. On September 7 the spot reading was $5.69. Committing to the same chip for a term cost less at every tenor: $5.73 for three months, $5.64 for six, and $5.39 for twelve. The market's forward rate — the price of a B200-hour at a future date, rather than a contract running to that date — sat at $5.68 three months out, $5.41 at six months, and $5.03 at twelve.

A curve shaped that way is called backwardated. Locking in a year of Blackwell capacity costs roughly 5% less per hour than renting spot today, and the twelve-month forward sits about 12% under the current index. Silicon Data is careful, correctly, to say this establishes what commitment costs now rather than what rates will do next summer. It is a quote, not a forecast. But it is the market's actual clearing price for the forward, and it points in one direction.

Read plainly: providers are currently willing to sell future Blackwell capacity cheaper than they sell capacity they have today. That is the opposite of what buyers were bracing for in a supply-constrained market, and it is the single most useful thing the new contracts reveal on day one.

The most recent readings reinforce the sense of stabilization rather than spike. The B200 index stood at $5.45 per GPU-hour on the portal, and the H100 neo-cloud index at $2.53. August was the quietest full month in the B200 series since it began in August 2025: every daily value sat between $5.58 and $5.69, a spread of 2.0%, with no day moving more than 1.2%.

...

The other thing the indices make measurable is how the chip generations price against each other. On July 27 the B200 index stood at $5.66 against an H100 neo-cloud rate of $2.75 — a premium of roughly 106%. On September 7 the portal showed B200 at $5.69 against H200 at $3.29 and H100 at $2.63, putting Blackwell at about 1.7 times the H200 and 2.2 times the H100.

...

The honest caveat is in the data itself: daily changes in the two series were essentially uncorrelated over the twelve-week window, so there is no support yet for claims that the rates move together. And a young index can widen as its provider panel matures. What is established is the level, the direction, and the size of the spread. Watching it monthly is now a public exercise rather than a private negotiation.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Dataset
highlights: A free, openly licensed (CC BY 4.0) dataset of posted cloud GPU rental prices across the whole market: GPU marketplaces, specialized GPU clouds, serverless platforms and hyperscale clouds. It contains a normalized snapshot of every current posted offer (provider, GPU model, VRAM, offer type, region, per-GPU-hour price, minimum GPU count, availability) and a daily price series with each day's lowest, average and highest posted price per provider and GPU. Every price is a rate a provider publishes. None is a transaction. This version (2026-10-04) holds the snapshot of 2026-10-04 06:50 UTC and the daily series from 2026-08-05 to 2026-10-04. It is the first version to carry corrections: three labelling errors found on 2026-10-03 (a preemptible rate recorded as on-demand at one provider, a PCIe card recorded under the SXM name at two) are listed in corrections.json, the daily series is published both corrected (gpu-prices-daily) and exactly as recorded (gpu-prices-daily-as-recorded), and no assumed price is filled in. Earlier versions hold days back to 2026-07-31 and predate these corrections. It also archives FastGPU's comment to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission on the Request for Comment on the Listing of Compute Derivatives Contracts (RIN 3038-AF77, 91 FR 54259), together with the script, inputs and output that reproduce every figure in that comment (cftc-rin-3038-AF77-replication.zip). Published and maintained by FastGPU, a live GPU price comparison service. Official dataset page and column documentation: https://fastgpu.co/dataset. Method: https://fastgpu.co/methodology.

results.title: GPU Futures Explained: CME H100 and B200 Contracts | Opengrid
highlights:
GPU compute is becoming something you can trade. CME Group lists H100 and B200 rental futures from 5 October 2026, built on Silicon Data's GPU rental price indices. ICE and Ornn have announced GPU compute futures of their own. This post explains what GPU futures are, why they are arriving now, who would use them, and what they still depend on.

...

The contracts don't hand you a GPU. They settle against a price index, a published reference price for renting a given chip. CME's H100 and B200 contracts are built on indices from Silicon Data, a company that publishes GPU rental price indices. If the index rises, a buyer of the future gains. If it falls, the seller gains.

## Why now: the price moves too much to ignore

A hedge is only worth having when the price moves. GPU prices now move by double digits in weeks:

| When | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Jun 2025 | AWS cut its H100 on-demand price 44% in a single announcement |
| Jun to Jul 2025 | Other providers followed with cuts of 20 to 25% in single moves |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | Silicon Data's H100 rental index rose from $2.00 to $2.20 in four weeks, up 10% |
| Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contract prices rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour, up about 40% |

And each chip moves on its own. In one stretch, H100 rose 10% while A100 and B200 stayed flat. For a team with a large training budget, or a GPU cloud with racks of capacity to fill, that is real financial risk. We cover the full price history in how GPU rental prices moved in 2025 and 2026.

...

## What futures still need: a liquid spot market

A futures market is only as good as the price it settles against. For oil, that price comes from huge volumes of physical barrels changing hands every day. For GPU compute, the spot market underneath is still fragmented:

- 209 GPU clouds, each with its own console, contract and API.
- The same H100 listing from about $1.25 to $11.07 an hour, depending on who you rent from.
- Aggregators reaching about 20 of those clouds, so most supply is outside any single view.

An index can sample list prices. But the strongest reference price comes from real transactions, real jobs placed at real prices across the whole market. The more on-demand compute changes hands through a neutral layer, the better the price that futures settle against.

results.title: GPU Cloud Aggregators & Marketplaces Compared (2026) | Opengrid
highlights:
SemiAnalysis tracks 209 GPU clouds, up from 124. Each one has its own console, contract, API and bill. Prices for the same chip vary widely: an on-demand H100 lists anywhere from about $1.25 to $11.07 an hour depending on the provider. Prices also move fast. AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement in June 2025, and one-year H100 contract prices then rose about 40% between October 2025 and March 2026.

...

Marketplaces sell GPU time from their own pool of supply, often at the low end of the price range. RunPod is a developer GPU cloud. SF Compute sells tradable blocks of GPU time. Mithril runs spot GPU auctions. Vast.ai is a marketplace where hosts list GPUs for rent. Developer clouds and marketplaces cluster at roughly $1.25 to $2.89 an hour for an on-demand H100.

Where they stop: each one sells its own pool of supply. None of them works across providers, so a better price or more capacity at another cloud is invisible from inside the marketplace.

results.title: H100 rental price — what clouds charge per GPU-hour
highlights:
The H100 rental price on the providers' own pricing pages runs from $1.78 to $11.06 per GPU-hour.

By Daniel Okafor 7 min read

The H100 rental price depends on the provider and on how you rent. On the providers’ own pricing pages, one Nvidia H100 ranged from $1.78 per GPU-hour, the lowest live ask on the Lium marketplace on October 19, 2026, to $11.06 on demand on Google Cloud, checked October 2. Among the clouds, CoreWeave spot was about $2.46, and Lambda and Nebius listed on-demand H100s at $3.99 and $4.50. These prices change often; the full, regularly re-checked list is on our cloud GPU price tracker.

...

Clouds publish H100 prices in two ways. Some list a price for a single GPU: Lambda shows its H100 SXM at $3.99 “/GPU/HR”, and Nebius lists the HGX H100 per GPU-hour. Others sell whole machines, usually eight H100s with CPUs, memory and local storage, and quote the machine’s hourly price. AWS, Google Cloud and CoreWeave do this.

...

On-demand is pay-as-you-go: you start and stop instances and pay by the hour at the list price. All of the per-GPU figures from Lambda, Nebius and Google Cloud in the table below are on-demand.

Spot is spare capacity sold at a discount, which the provider can take back when it needs it. CoreWeave lists its HGX H100 instance at $19.71 an hour on spot against $49.24 on demand, or $2.46 versus $6.155 per GPU-hour.

Reserved and committed capacity trades flexibility for a lower or guaranteed rate. CoreWeave says committed usage brings “up to 60% discounts” on its on-demand prices. Google Cloud offers committed use discounts on its A3 machines; it says these machine types are not eligible for sustained use discounts or flexible committed use discounts.

...

| Provider | Offer | Billing | Listed price | Per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lium | H100 80GB HBM3 (SXM), marketplace, lowest live ask | On-demand, billed per second | from $1.78 per GPU-hour (checked October 19, 2026) | $1.78 |
| CoreWeave | HGX H100, 8 GPUs, North America | Spot | $19.71 per instance-hour | $2.46 |
| Lambda | H100 SXM 80 GB | On-demand | $3.99 per GPU-hour | $3.99 |
| Nebius | HGX H100 | On-demand | $4.50 per GPU-hour (effective October 1, 2026) | $4.50 |
| AWS | p5.48xlarge Capacity Block, US East (N. Virginia) | Reserved, paid up front | $41.528 per instance-hour | $5.191 |
| CoreWeave | HGX H100, 8 GPUs, North America | On-demand | $49.24 per instance-hour | $6.155 |
| Google Cloud | a3-highgpu-8g, Iowa (us-central1) | On-demand | $88.49 per instance-hour | $11.06 |

Prices move in both directions and sometimes within days. Nebius’s table shows the HGX H100 at $3.85 per GPU-hour in its previous on-demand column and $4.50 in the column effective October 1, 2026. AWS’s P5 Capacity Block rate changes on October 7. Treat the table as a dated snapshot and check the cloud GPU price tracker for the current figures, which also cover Azure, RunPod, DigitalOcean, Crusoe, Hyperstack and other providers.

...

A GPU-hour price is rarely the whole bill.

- Tax. Lambda states its prices are “plus applicable sales tax/VAT/GST.” Most list prices are quoted before tax.
- Data transfer. CoreWeave says it charges “no ingress, egress, or transfer fees,” and Lambda advertises no egress fees. On clouds that do charge for data transfer, the charge is billed separately from the GPU-hour.
- Storage. Local SSD is part of several of the instance prices above, but persistent or network storage for datasets and checkpoints is priced separately.
- Operating system and software. AWS bills the Capacity Block operating system fee separately from the reservation fee, and lists different OS fees for Linux, RHEL, SLES and Ubuntu Pro.
- Region. Hyperscaler prices are per region. The AWS and Google Cloud figures above are for US East (N. Virginia) and Iowa respectively; other regions list different rates.

...

Start with the per-GPU-hour figure, then check four things: what is bundled with the GPU (vCPUs, RAM, local disk), which H100 variant it is, how long you must commit and whether you pay in advance, and what transfer, storage and tax charges apply on top. A spot price is the lowest cloud list price in the table but suits only jobs that can stop and resume. A Capacity Block guarantees GPUs for a set window but is paid up front.

results.title: How to Choose (and Switch) GPU Cloud Providers | Opengrid
highlights:
There are a lot of options, and they are spread far apart:

- 209 GPU clouds. SemiAnalysis tracks 209 GPU clouds, up from 124. Each has its own console, contract, API and bill.
- Prices spread across a wide band. An on-demand H100 lists from about $1.25 an hour at developer clouds and marketplaces to $11.07 an hour at the most expensive hyperscaler. The same is true of other chips: A100s range from $1.09 to $5.07 an hour and B200s from $3.50 to $27.04.
- Reliability varies a lot. SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX 2.0 grades GPU clouds from Platinum down to Underperforming. Only one is rated Platinum.
- Capacity is tight. SemiAnalysis reported in 2026 that on-demand capacity was sold out across all GPU types, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027.

...

So teams pick once and overpay for as long as they stay. That made sense when prices barely moved. It makes less sense now. AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement in June 2025. Then one-year H100 contract prices rose about 40% between October 2025 and March 2026. The right provider this quarter is often the wrong one next quarter. More on that in how GPU rental prices moved in 2025 and 2026.

...

### 3. Benchmark the price against the market

Compare the quote with the whole band for that chip, not just two or three providers. Rough H100 on-demand bands as of September 2026:

| Provider type | Examples | H100 on-demand, per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hyperscalers | Google Cloud, Oracle, Azure, AWS | $6.88 to $11.07 |
| Neoclouds | CoreWeave, Crusoe, Nebius, Lambda | $3.29 to $6.16 |
| Developer clouds and marketplaces | RunPod, Together, Vast.ai, Lium | $1.25 to $2.89 |

...

Spot capacity runs 60 to 91% below on-demand, but it can be pulled in the middle of a job. Spot suits jobs that checkpoint often or can restart. Long training runs with no checkpointing belong on on-demand or reserved capacity.
